title: Teeth: two sets for a lifetime, and what wears them away

summary.text: Tooth enamel is the hardest part of your body, yet a sour drink can slowly wear it away. In this unit you drop pieces of eggshell into water, sugar water, milk, lemon juice and vinegar, and see which ones fizz and go soft. You find out why you get 20 milk teeth and then up to 32 adult teeth, and what the four kinds of teeth do. Then you learn how saliva, fluoride and brushing keep the teeth you have for life.
summary.art: Five clear glasses in a row on a kitchen counter, each with a small piece of eggshell, and tiny bubbles rising from the shell in the last two glasses, with a child looking closely.

intro.hook: Hold a clean piece of eggshell. Press it gently with your thumb. It is hard. Your tooth enamel is even harder. Could a drink from your kitchen make something so hard go soft?
intro.text: Enamel is the white outside layer of your teeth. It is the hardest part of your whole body, harder than bone. An eggshell is hard too, and it is made with calcium, like enamel. So an eggshell is a good stand-in for a tooth in a test. Before you read on, guess. Which drink would harm a hard shell: sugar water, or lemon juice? Say why you think so. You are going to find out.
intro.art: A child's hand holding a curved piece of white eggshell next to a smiling mouth with white teeth, and a lemon and a bowl of sugar on the table.

outcomes: By the end I can say that children have 20 milk teeth, and grown-ups have up to 32 adult teeth that grow in the jaw underneath.
By the end I can name incisors, canines, premolars and molars, and say the job of each one.
By the end I can name the enamel, dentine, pulp and root of a tooth.
By the end I can test which kitchen liquids make an eggshell fizz and go soft, and say what that shows about acid and teeth.
By the end I can say where acid in the mouth comes from, and three ways to look after my teeth.
By the end I can guess first, give a reason, and then say what my test showed.

terms.meaning: The first set of teeth. A child has 20 of them. They fall out one by one, usually between about age 6 and age 12.
terms.example: Most children lose their two bottom front milk teeth first, at about age 6 or 7.
terms.art: A small child's smile with 20 small, very white teeth and one gap at the bottom front.

terms.meaning: The second set of teeth. They grow in the jaw under the milk teeth and come out as the milk teeth fall. A grown-up has up to 32. These teeth are never replaced.
terms.example: A new adult front tooth is bigger than the milk tooth it replaced, and its edge has three tiny bumps.
terms.art: A new adult front tooth coming up in a gap, larger than the milk teeth beside it, with a wavy bottom edge.

terms.meaning: The thin, flat teeth at the front of the mouth. Their sharp edge bites and cuts food.
terms.example: You bite a piece off a guava with your incisors.
terms.art: A smile with the four top and four bottom front teeth coloured blue.

terms.meaning: The pointed teeth at each corner of the front teeth. They grip and tear food.
terms.example: You hold a piece of chewy dosa with your canines and pull to tear it.
terms.art: A smile with the four pointed corner teeth coloured yellow.

terms.meaning: The two teeth on each side just behind the canines, in grown-ups. They have two points on top and help to crush food. Children do not have them yet.
terms.example: When a child's back milk teeth fall out, premolars grow in their place.
terms.art: A grown-up's teeth with the two teeth behind each canine coloured orange.

terms.meaning: The wide, bumpy teeth at the back of the mouth. They grind and crush food into a soft paste.
terms.example: Your molars grind a mouthful of rice and sambar before you swallow.
terms.art: A wide back tooth with little hills and valleys on top, coloured green.

terms.meaning: The hard, white, shiny outside layer of a tooth. It is the hardest material in the human body.
terms.example: When you tap your teeth together, enamel is what clicks.
terms.art: A tooth cut in half, with its thin white outer layer shown bright and shiny.

terms.meaning: The pale yellow layer under the enamel. It is softer than enamel and makes up most of a tooth.
terms.example: Grown-up teeth often look a little more yellow than milk teeth, because the dentine shows through.
terms.art: A tooth cut in half, with the thick pale yellow layer under the white enamel shown.

terms.meaning: The soft, living middle of a tooth. It has blood vessels and nerves. Nerves carry feelings, such as cold or pain, to the brain.
terms.example: When you drink very cold water and a tooth tingles, the nerves in the pulp are sensing the cold.
terms.art: A tooth cut in half, with a soft pink middle and thin red and white lines running down into the root.

terms.meaning: The part of a tooth hidden inside the jaw, under the gum. It holds the tooth in place.
terms.example: An adult molar has two or three long roots, like the legs of a stool.
terms.art: A tooth drawn with the gum line marked, the white crown above and the long roots below in the jaw.

terms.meaning: The soft pink skin that covers the jaw bone round the bottom of each tooth.
terms.example: If you brush too hard, your gums can get sore.
terms.art: A smile with the pink gums around the teeth highlighted.

terms.meaning: A kind of substance that tastes sour. Strong acids can wear away hard things made with calcium, like eggshell and tooth enamel.
terms.example: Lemon juice, vinegar, tamarind and raw mango are sour because they have acids in them.
terms.art: A lemon, a bottle of vinegar, a ball of tamarind and a raw mango slice, each with a small sour face.

terms.meaning: A soft, sticky, pale layer that builds up on teeth. It is full of tiny living beings called bacteria, too small to see one by one.
terms.example: The fuzzy feeling on your teeth in the morning is plaque.
terms.art: A tooth close up, with a thin creamy layer near the gum, and a zoom circle showing many tiny round and rod-shaped bacteria.

terms.meaning: A hole in a tooth, made when acid wears away the enamel and the dentine.
terms.example: A dentist can see a cavity as a dark spot and fill it.
terms.art: A molar with a small dark hole in one of the valleys on top.

terms.meaning: The watery juice your mouth makes all day. It washes food away, and it slowly washes acid away too.
terms.example: Your mouth waters when you smell hot pakoras. That water is saliva.
terms.art: A child sniffing a plate of pakoras, with a little speech bubble saying 'my mouth is watering'.

terms.meaning: A substance found in small amounts in water, tea and most toothpaste. A little of it makes enamel harder for acid to wear away.
terms.example: The tube of toothpaste at home probably says 'fluoride' on the side.
terms.art: A toothpaste tube with the word fluoride circled on the side, and a pea-sized blob of paste on a child's brush.

terms.meaning: A doctor for teeth and gums.
terms.example: A dentist uses a small round mirror on a stick to see the back of your teeth.
terms.art: A woman dentist holding a small round mirror on a stick, smiling at a child in the dentist's chair.

explanations.context: This card explains why you get one set of teeth as a small child and a second set later.
explanations.definition: Humans grow two sets of teeth: 20 milk teeth, and later up to 32 adult teeth.
explanations.description: A baby's milk teeth start to come through the gums at about 6 months old. By about age 3, all 20 are in. A small jaw only has room for small teeth. As you grow, your jaw gets bigger. Adult teeth are bigger, so they fit the bigger jaw. The adult teeth form inside the jaw, under the milk teeth, years before they come out. Between about age 6 and 12, the milk teeth fall out one by one, and adult teeth take their place. Most grown-ups end up with 28 to 32 teeth.
examples: A child of 4 usually has all 20 milk teeth.
A child of 7 often has a gap at the front, and a new, bigger tooth coming up in it.
At about age 6, the first adult molars come in at the very back, behind the milk teeth. No milk tooth falls out to make room for them.
Wisdom teeth are the last molars. They may come in at about 17 to 25 years old, or never.
explanations.art: A row of four mouths: a baby with no teeth, a child of 3 with 20 small teeth, a child of 7 with a gap and a big new tooth, and a grown-up with 32 teeth.

explanations.concept: How a milk tooth falls out
explanations.context: This card explains why a milk tooth gets wobbly and then falls out.
explanations.definition: As an adult tooth grows up from inside the jaw, the body slowly dissolves the root of the milk tooth above it. With almost no root left, the milk tooth wobbles and falls out.
explanations.description: A milk tooth has a root that holds it in the jaw. Under it, an adult tooth is growing. As the adult tooth moves up, the body slowly takes away the milk tooth's root. Dissolve means to break down into tiny pieces that are carried away. A milk tooth with only a short root left cannot stay firm, so it wobbles. That is why a fallen milk tooth has hardly any root. The root did not break off. It was taken away, bit by bit, to make room.
examples: Look at a fallen milk tooth, if your family kept one. The bottom is short and rough, with no long root.
Sometimes the adult tooth comes up behind the milk tooth instead of under it. Then a child has two rows for a while, and a dentist may help the milk tooth come out.
explanations.art: A drawing of a jaw cut open from the side: a small milk tooth on top with a short, worn-away root, and a big adult tooth growing just under it.

explanations.concept: Four kinds of teeth, four jobs
explanations.context: This card explains the kinds of teeth in your mouth and what each kind does.
explanations.definition: Incisors bite and cut, canines grip and tear, premolars crush, and molars grind.
explanations.description: Food goes on a journey across your teeth. The flat front incisors bite a piece off. The pointed canines grip and tear tough food. Your tongue then pushes the piece to the back. There the wide, bumpy molars grind it into a soft paste you can swallow. Grown-ups also have premolars between the canines and the molars. Children do not have premolars yet. When a child's back milk molars fall out, premolars grow in their place. The new adult molars come in further back.
examples: Biting a piece off a banana: incisors.
Tearing a piece of chewy roti or dosa: canines.
Grinding roasted chana: molars, and in grown-ups premolars too.
explanations.art: A big friendly drawing of a mouth with the incisors blue, canines yellow, premolars orange and molars green, and a small arrow showing food moving from front to back.

explanations.context: This card explains the layers of a tooth, from the hard outside to the living middle.
explanations.definition: A tooth has a hard outer layer of enamel, a layer of dentine under it, and soft living pulp in the middle. The root holds it in the jaw.
explanations.description: The part of a tooth you can see is called the crown. Its outside is enamel. Enamel is mostly hard minerals, with calcium in them. Under the enamel is dentine, which is softer and pale yellow. In the middle is the pulp. The pulp is alive. It has blood vessels that bring food and nerves that sense heat, cold and pain. The cells that made the enamel are gone once a tooth comes out. So a deep hole in enamel cannot grow back. A dentist has to fill it.
examples: A tooth tingles when you drink something very cold, because the nerves in the pulp sense it.
A chipped front tooth stays chipped, because enamel does not grow back.
explanations.art: A large tooth cut in half from top to bottom, showing white enamel, yellow dentine, pink pulp and two roots inside the jaw bone under the gum.

explanations.context: This card explains what acid does to hard things like eggshell and teeth. It comes after the eggshell test.
explanations.definition: Acids can dissolve hard materials made with calcium, like eggshell and tooth enamel, a little at a time.
explanations.description: In the eggshell test, vinegar and lemon juice made tiny bubbles on the shell. By the next day, the shell in vinegar had gone soft. An eggshell is made of a material with calcium in it. The acid in vinegar breaks that material down, and the bubbles are a gas that comes out as it breaks. Tooth enamel is a different material from eggshell, and harder. But it has calcium in it too, and acid can dissolve it slowly. Enamel does not make bubbles as it dissolves. Water, milk and sugar water did not make the shell fizz.
examples: Vinegar and lemon juice made bubbles on the eggshell.
Sour foods and drinks, such as lemon juice, tamarind, raw mango and fizzy drinks, have acids in them.
A tooth is not dropped in vinegar for a day. But a sour sip every hour gives acid many small chances to work.
explanations.art: A zoom picture: a piece of eggshell in vinegar with bubbles rising, beside a tooth with a thin worn patch on its enamel.

explanations.concept: Where acid in the mouth comes from
explanations.context: This card explains the two places the acid that harms teeth comes from.
explanations.definition: Acid in the mouth comes from sour food and drinks, and from bacteria in plaque, who make acid as they eat sugar.
explanations.description: The sugar water in our test did not fizz on the eggshell. So how does sugar harm teeth? Your mouth is home to many kinds of tiny living beings called bacteria. Some of them live in plaque on your teeth. They sense sugar and gather where it is. As they eat it, they make acid, right on your teeth. After a sweet snack, they keep making acid for about half an hour or more. So sugar wears teeth through the acid that bacteria make as they eat sugar. How often you eat sugar matters more than how much at one time.
examples: One sweet after lunch gives the bacteria one acid time. Five small sweets through the afternoon give them five.
Sticky sweets like toffee and chikki stay on teeth for longer, so the bacteria have sugar for longer.

perspectives.explanation: They describe mouth bacteria in terms of chemistry: the bacteria take in sugar, break the sugar down for energy, and give out acid as waste. They do not use words like sense or choose.

perspectives.who: Biologists who study how bacteria sense
perspectives.explanation: Bacteria do sense the world. They detect sugar and other chemicals, signal to each other, and change what they do together when there are many of them.

explanations.art: A tooth with a thin layer of plaque, and a zoom circle showing tiny bacteria gathered round grains of sugar, with small acid drops around them.

explanations.context: This card explains what saliva, fluoride and brushing each do for your teeth.
explanations.definition: Saliva washes acid away and puts minerals back into enamel. Fluoride makes enamel harder for acid to wear. Brushing takes away plaque.
explanations.description: After acid has worked on a tooth, saliva slowly washes the acid away. It also carries calcium back into the enamel, which can repair the very first soft spot. A little fluoride makes enamel harder for acid to dissolve. That is why most toothpaste has fluoride in it. Brushing twice a day, in the morning and before bed, takes away the plaque where the bacteria live. Use a soft brush and a pea-sized blob of fluoride toothpaste. Brush gently for about two minutes, and spit the foam out.
examples: Drinking plain water after a snack rinses food away.
Eating sweets with a meal, not between meals, gives fewer acid times.
Brushing gently is better than brushing hard, because hard brushing can hurt the gums.
A dentist checks teeth and can fill a small cavity before it grows.
explanations.art: Three small helpers drawn as pictures: a drop of saliva, a pea-sized blob of toothpaste on a soft brush, and a glass of water, all around a happy tooth.

explanations.context: This card explains why a little fluoride helps teeth, but too much does not.
explanations.definition: A small amount of fluoride makes enamel stronger. Too much fluoride while teeth are forming leaves white or brown spots on them. This is called dental fluorosis.
explanations.description: Fluoride comes naturally from some rocks into well and borewell water. In some parts of India, such as Nalgonda in Telangana and parts of Rajasthan, the ground water has too much fluoride. Many children there grow teeth with brown spots. Very large amounts over many years can harm bones too. So the amount matters. This is why young children use only a small blob of toothpaste and spit it out, instead of swallowing it.
examples: A pea-sized blob of toothpaste is enough for a child aged 3 to 6.
Some villages with high-fluoride water now get treated water from pipes.
explanations.art: Two smiles side by side: one with plain white teeth, and one with small brown spots on the front teeth, with a borewell pump in the background.

explanations.concept: Why humans get only two sets
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists are still working on: why we do not grow new teeth again and again.
explanations.description: Humans and most other mammals grow two sets of teeth. Sharks and crocodiles replace their teeth many times over their lives. An elephant grows six sets of big molars, one after another. Scientists have ideas about why mammals settled on two sets. One idea is that our upper and lower teeth fit together very exactly, and swapping them again and again would spoil that fit. Nobody knows for sure. Some scientists in Japan are now testing a medicine that may help a person grow a missing tooth. We do not yet know if it works.
examples: A shark has rows of spare teeth waiting behind the front row.
An elephant's last set of molars must last the rest of her life.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how mammals grew from earlier animals
perspectives.explanation: Many think mammals' teeth became so carefully shaped to fit together that only one swap, from child to adult, was worth the cost.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how teeth grow
perspectives.explanation: They point out that the jaw seems to keep some of the signals for making new teeth. They are testing whether those signals can be switched on again.

explanations.art: A shark with rows of teeth, a crocodile, an elephant showing a big flat molar, and a child with a gap-toothed smile, all side by side.

agreed.text: Humans have two sets of teeth: 20 milk teeth, then up to 32 adult teeth.
agreed.evidence: Dentists all over the world see the same pattern. X-ray pictures of a child's jaw show the adult teeth already formed under the milk teeth.

agreed.text: Tooth decay is caused by acid, from sour food and drink and from bacteria in plaque who eat sugar.
agreed.evidence: Pieces of tooth in acid go soft in a laboratory. Teeth kept clean of plaque, and fed sugar less often, get fewer cavities.

agreed.text: A little fluoride makes enamel harder for acid to wear away, and too much spots the teeth.
agreed.evidence: Towns with a little fluoride in their water had fewer cavities. Places with a lot, like parts of Nalgonda, have many children with spotted teeth.

agreed.text: Enamel is the hardest material in the human body, and a deep hole in it does not grow back.
agreed.evidence: The cells that make enamel are gone once a tooth comes through the gum. Dentists fill cavities because they do not heal.

agreed.text: People have cared for teeth for thousands of years.
agreed.evidence: At Mehrgarh, an old farming village in South Asia, scientists found back teeth with small holes drilled in them, from about 9,000 to 7,500 years ago. They are among the oldest drilled teeth ever found.

challenging.claim: Milk teeth do not matter, because they fall out anyway.
challenging.for: Milk teeth do fall out, and adult teeth take their place.
challenging.against: A child uses milk teeth for chewing and speaking for up to 8 years. A milk tooth with a deep cavity can hurt and can be infected. Milk teeth also hold the space for the adult teeth underneath.
challenging.context: This card is about a belief many families hold about milk teeth.

challenging.claim: Sugar eats holes in teeth by itself.
challenging.for: People who eat sugar often get more cavities.
challenging.against: In the eggshell test, sugar water did not fizz on the shell. Sugar harms teeth because bacteria in plaque eat sugar and make acid. Without the bacteria, sugar alone does very little to enamel.
challenging.context: This card is about a guess many children make before the eggshell test.

challenging.for: Scrubbing hard cleans a dirty pot.
challenging.against: Plaque is soft and comes off with gentle brushing. Hard brushing can hurt the gums and wear down the teeth near the gums over the years.
challenging.context: This card is about how hard to brush.

challenging.claim: A neem or babool twig cleans teeth as well as a toothbrush.
challenging.who: Many families in India, and some dentists
challenging.for: People in India have cleaned their teeth with chewed twigs, called datun, for a very long time. Old Indian medical books describe it. Neem has substances that slow down some bacteria. Some studies found twigs used well clean about as well as a brush.
challenging.against: A twig is hard to use well on the back teeth. It has no fluoride, unless used with toothpaste. Studies are small and do not all agree.
challenging.context: This card is about the twig toothbrush used in India for a very long time.

challenging.claim: You should wait a while after a sour drink before you brush.
challenging.for: Right after an acid drink, the outside of the enamel is a little softer, so brushing at once might wear more of it away.
challenging.against: Other studies found that brushing soon after does little harm, especially with fluoride toothpaste. Scientists still argue about how long to wait, if at all.
challenging.context: This card is about when to brush after a sour drink.

big_questions.q: Why did vinegar make the eggshell fizz, but sugar water did not?
big_questions.hint: Think about what acid does to things made with calcium. Does sugar taste sour?

big_questions.q: Your adult teeth were inside your jaw before you could walk. How did your body know when to let them come out?
big_questions.hint: Nobody knows all of the answer. The jaw sends signals, and the root of the milk tooth is taken away first.

big_questions.q: The bacteria in your mouth eat your leftovers and make acid. Are they guests, pests or partners?
big_questions.hint: Many mouth bacteria are harmless or even helpful. Only some make a lot of acid.

big_questions.q: A shark grows new teeth again and again. Would you want to? What would be good and what would be hard?
big_questions.hint: Think of the fit between your top and bottom teeth.

big_questions.q: Your teeth are made with calcium from your food, and that calcium came from rocks long ago. Is a part of a mountain now in your smile?
big_questions.hint: Calcium moves from rock to soil to plant to animal to you.

story.title: The Tooth With No Root
story.note: Kavya, Ammamma, Arjun and Amma are made up. In many parts of India, and in many other countries, some families throw a fallen milk tooth onto a roof. Others bury it or keep it. Ammamma is the Telugu word many children use for their mother's mother.
text: Kavya was seven. She lived on the fourth floor of a block of flats in Hyderabad, with her mother, her little brother Arjun, and her grandmother. Kavya called her grandmother Ammamma.

For two weeks, one of Kavya's bottom front teeth had been wobbly. She pushed it with her tongue all day. She pushed it at school. She pushed it while she brushed. It went forward and back, forward and back, like a door in the wind.
One evening, Ammamma cut a guava into pieces and sprinkled a little salt and chilli powder on top. Kavya took a big bite. Something went click. She stopped chewing.
She spat the bite into her hand. There, in the middle of the pink guava, was a tiny white tooth.
'Ammamma! It came out!' said Kavya.
Arjun came running. He was five, and all his teeth were still tight. 'Let me see! Let me see!'
Kavya rinsed the tooth under the tap and held it up to the light. It was very small. The top was smooth and white. But the bottom was short and rough, as if someone had nibbled it.
Kavya's face fell. 'Ammamma, the root broke off. It's still stuck inside my gum!'
Ammamma put on her glasses and looked at the tooth. Then she looked at the gap in Kavya's mouth, with the torch from the kitchen drawer.
'Nothing is stuck,' said Ammamma. 'This tooth never lost its root by breaking. Your body took the root away, slowly, bit by bit.'
'Why would my body do that?' asked Kavya.
'Because a new tooth is coming,' said Ammamma. 'Look closely, right in the gap.'
Kavya went to the mirror. Ammamma held the torch. Deep in the gap, under the pink gum, Kavya could just see something white. It was the edge of a new tooth.

'Your adult tooth was growing inside your jaw all this time,' said Ammamma. 'It was there when you were Arjun's age. As it moved up, your body dissolved the root of the milk tooth above it. Dissolve means break down into tiny pieces that get carried away. When almost no root was left, the milk tooth wobbled, and the guava did the rest.'
Arjun opened his mouth as wide as it would go. 'Do I have new teeth inside too?'
'Yes,' said Ammamma. 'You have twenty milk teeth now, and new teeth are waiting under them. Grown-ups end up with up to thirty-two.'
'Thirty-two!' said Arjun. 'Where do they all fit?'
'Your jaw grows bigger, so bigger teeth can fit,' said Ammamma. 'And some new ones come in at the very back, where there were no milk teeth at all.'
Kavya thought about this. 'Will my new teeth fall out too, when I am big?'

Ammamma laughed and tapped her own front teeth. 'No. You get only two sets. Your new teeth have to last you your whole life. I have had mine for sixty years. Two of them have fillings, because I ate too many sweets when I was young, all day long.'

Over the next three weeks, Kavya watched the new tooth come up. Every morning she checked it in the mirror. It was bigger than the milk teeth beside it. It was a little more cream-coloured than white. And its edge was not straight. It had three tiny bumps, like a little wave.
'Ammamma, my new tooth is wavy,' she said.
'All new front teeth have those bumps,' said Ammamma. 'They wear smooth as you bite, over a few years. Look at Amma's front teeth. Hers are flat.'
Kavya checked. It was true.
'What do we do with the old tooth?' asked Kavya. 'Meena at school said her grandmother threw hers on the roof.'
'When I was a girl in our village near Nellore, we threw them on the roof too,' said Ammamma. 'But our building has ten floors, and the door to the roof is locked. What would you like to do?'
Kavya found a small empty box from a pair of earrings. She put cotton inside, and laid the milk tooth on top. On the lid she wrote: 'My first milk tooth. The root was taken away to make room.'

That night, Kavya brushed her teeth very gently round the gap. Arjun brushed his too, extra carefully. 'These have to last me till my new ones come,' he said. 'And then the new ones have to last forever.'
story.epiphany: The new tooth was growing inside my jaw all along. My body took away the milk tooth's root to make room for it, so a milk tooth falls out with no root.
ask: Why did Kavya's milk tooth have no long root?
Where was Kavya's new tooth before the milk tooth fell out?
How was the new tooth different from the milk teeth beside it?
Why did Ammamma say the new teeth have to last a whole life?
art: A girl at a kitchen table in a city flat holding a tiny white milk tooth on her palm next to a cut guava, while her grandmother in glasses leans in with a torch and a small boy peers over.
The same girl at a mirror pulling her lip down to show a new tooth with a wavy edge coming up in the gap, and a small open earring box with cotton and a milk tooth inside.

rules: Cut out the cards. Give each player one set of 4 tooth cards. Put the 12 food job cards face down in a pile.
One player turns over the top food card and reads it aloud, but not the back.
On the count of three, every player holds up the tooth card that does that job.
Turn the food card over and read the back. Every player who held up the right tooth card gets one point.
If someone held up a different card, they may say why. If everyone agrees that tooth also does the job, they get a point too.
Take turns to read the next card. After all 12 cards, the player with the most points wins.
