flow.kid: Read the food card. Which teeth do that job? Hold up the card.
flow.parent: Children may say they crush peanuts with molars. That is right for them, because they have no premolars yet. Give them the point and say why.

check.q: Which teeth tear a piece off a chewy dosa?
check.why: Canines are pointed, so they grip and tear. If you picked molars, remember that molars grind food at the back, after it has been torn off.

flow.context: This is the end of the game.
flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Which card was hardest? Why do you think humans have all four kinds?
flow.kid: Which card was hardest? Why do we need four kinds of teeth?

ask.q: Why do humans have all four kinds of teeth?
good: Because we eat many kinds of food.
Some food needs biting, some tearing and some grinding.

games.title: Acid Time or Helper?
games.context: This is a card game about what happens to teeth during a day. Each card shows a moment. Players decide if it gives teeth an acid time or helps them, and say why.

items.f: Sipping a sweet, fizzy drink slowly all afternoon
items.b: Acid time. Sugar for the bacteria, and acid in the drink, again and again for hours.

items.f: Brushing teeth before bed with fluoride toothpaste
items.b: Helper. It takes away plaque and makes enamel harder for acid.

items.f: Drinking a glass of plain water after lunch
items.b: Helper. Water rinses food away and has no sugar or acid.

items.f: Sucking a toffee slowly in class
items.b: Acid time. A toffee keeps sugar on the teeth for a long time.

items.f: Eating raw mango with salt and chilli
items.b: Acid time. Raw mango is sour, so it has acid.

items.f: Eating a crunchy carrot stick
items.b: Helper. It has little sugar, and chewing makes plenty of saliva.

items.f: Going to the dentist for a check-up
items.b: Helper. A dentist can find a small cavity before it grows.

items.f: Eating payasam at the end of a meal
items.b: Acid time, but only one. Eating a sweet with a meal is better than eating it later on its own.

items.f: Nibbling biscuits one by one all evening
items.b: Acid time. Many small snacks give the bacteria many acid times.

items.f: Your mouth watering when you smell food
items.b: Helper. Saliva washes acid away and puts minerals back in enamel.

items.f: Brushing very hard with a hard brush
items.b: Neither. It does not clean better, and it can hurt the gums. Brush gently.

items.f: Squeezing lemon on your poha
items.b: Acid time. Lemon juice is sour. Eaten with a meal, it is one short acid time.

items.f: Spitting out the toothpaste foam, not rinsing a lot
items.b: Helper. A little fluoride stays on your teeth.

items.f: Falling asleep with milk with sugar in it still in your mouth
items.b: Acid time. Your mouth makes less saliva at night, so acid stays longer.

items.f: Chewing a piece of sugarcane
items.b: Acid time. Sugarcane juice is sugar, for the bacteria to eat.

items.f: Ending a meal with a few roasted peanuts
items.b: Helper. Peanuts have little sugar, and chewing them makes plenty of saliva.

rules: Cut out the 16 cards. Shuffle them and put them face down in a pile.
One player turns over the top card and reads the front aloud.
Every player puts a thumb up for 'helper', or a thumb down for 'acid time'. A flat hand means 'neither'.
Read the back of the card. Every player who was right gets one point.
The player who read the card says one way to turn an acid-time moment into a better one. If they can, they get one more point.
Take turns to read. After all 16 cards, the player with the most points wins.

setup.art: A pile of moment cards face down in the middle of a mat, with two girls and a boy sitting round it.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the moment cards. Put them in a pile.

setup.art: A girl reading a card, while one player shows a thumb up and two players show a thumb down.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Thumbs up for helper, thumbs down for acid time.

flow.context: This is the start of the acid time game.
flow.do: 1. Cut out and shuffle the cards. 2. Show the three hand signs.
flow.say: Thumb up means it helps your teeth. Thumb down means it gives your teeth an acid time. A flat hand means neither.
flow.kid: Thumb up is helper. Thumb down is acid time. Flat hand is neither.

flow.context: In this step you play the game.
flow.do: 1. Take turns reading a card. 2. Everyone shows a sign. 3. Read the back and give points. 4. The reader suggests a better moment.
flow.say: Is that a helper or an acid time? Show me. Now, how could we make it better?
flow.kid: Read the card. Thumb up or down? How could it be better?
flow.parent: Remember the eggshell test, if you have done it. Sour things made the shell fizz. Sugar works through the bacteria.

check.q: Which is worse for teeth: one sweet after lunch, or five sweets eaten one by one all afternoon?
options: Five sweets one by one all afternoon
check.why: Each time you eat sugar, the bacteria make acid for about half an hour or more. Five sweets at different times give five acid times. If you picked 'the same', remember that how often matters more than how much.

flow.context: This is the end of the game.
flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Which card surprised you? Why?
flow.kid: Which card surprised you? Why?

good: Brushing hard is not a helper.
Payasam with a meal is only one acid time.
Spitting is better than rinsing.

experiments.title: The Eggshell Test: which drinks make a hard shell go soft?
experiments.context: In this experiment you drop pieces of eggshell into five kitchen liquids: water, sugar water, milk, lemon juice and vinegar. You watch for bubbles. The next day, you feel each piece to see if it has stayed hard. Eggshell is made with calcium, like tooth enamel, so it is a stand-in for a tooth.
experiments.question: Which kitchen liquids make a hard eggshell fizz and go soft? Does sugar water harm it?
experiments.predict: Feel a piece of eggshell. Look at the five cups. Which ones do you think will harm the shell, and which will not? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every piece of shell is about the same size, about as big as your thumbnail. Every cup gets the same amount of liquid, 3 tablespoons. All the pieces go in at the same time and stay for the same time, until the same time the next day. Only the liquid is different. The cup of plain water shows what happens when nothing sour or sweet is added.
results_table: My guess: will it harm the shell?
Bubbles in the first 2 minutes? (lots, a few, none)
Next day: hard, or soft and bendy?

materials.item: the shell of one egg, washed in water and dried. If your family does not use eggs, ask a neighbour for one clean shell, or use 5 small cowrie shells or seashells
5 clear glasses, or clear plastic cups, or small empty jam jars
white vinegar, the kind used for cooking
lemon juice, squeezed from 2 lemons
milk
sugar water: 1 teaspoon of sugar stirred into 3 tablespoons of water
plain water
5 small paper labels, a pen and sticky tape
a tablespoon, a teaspoon and a torch
a plate or a piece of cardboard to cover the glasses overnight

experiments.safety: Vinegar and lemon juice sting in the eyes and in cuts. Keep fingers away from the eyes, and wash hands after the test. Do not drink the liquids at the end.

schedule.what: Guess. Set up the five glasses. Drop in the shells and watch for bubbles. Write down what you see. Cover the glasses.
Take out each piece of shell. Rinse it and press it gently. Is it hard, or soft and bendy? Say what you found.

experiments.record: Write your guess and your reason at the top. Fill in the results table. Draw each glass, with bubbles if you saw them. On day 2, circle the pieces that went soft.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: A little soft at the edges

setup.art: Five clear glasses in a row on a counter, each with a paper label: water, sugar water, milk, lemon juice, vinegar.
setup.caption: 1. Label five glasses. Pour 3 tablespoons of each liquid.

setup.art: A child's fingers dropping a thumbnail-sized piece of eggshell into each glass.
setup.caption: 2. Drop one piece of shell into each glass at the same time.

setup.art: A torch shining from the side of the vinegar glass, showing tiny bubbles stuck to the shell and rising.
setup.caption: 3. Shine a torch from the side. Look for bubbles.

setup.art: A child's fingers gently bending a soft piece of shell taken from the vinegar, next to a hard piece from the water.
setup.caption: 4. Next day: rinse each piece. Is it hard, or soft and bendy?

flow.context: This is the first step of the eggshell test. You feel the shell and guess what each liquid will do.
flow.do: 1. Give your child a piece of eggshell to feel and press. 2. Show the five liquids. 3. Ask the question below. 4. Write down their guess for each liquid, and their reason.
flow.say: Press the shell. It is hard, like a tooth. Which of these liquids will harm it? Which will not? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Press the shell. It is hard, like a tooth. Which drinks will harm it? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will harm the shell?
good: Sugar water, because sugar is bad for teeth.
Lemon juice, because it is sour and it stings.
Water will not, because we drink water all the time.

flow.parent: Don't say if the guess is right. Many children guess sugar water. That is a good guess with a reason, and the test will answer it.

flow.context: In this step you set up the five glasses for the eggshell test.
flow.do: 1. Stick a label on each glass: water, sugar water, milk, lemon juice, vinegar. 2. Pour 3 tablespoons of each liquid into its glass. 3. Break the eggshell into 5 pieces, each about the size of a thumbnail.
flow.say: Every glass gets the same amount, and every piece is about the same size. Then only the liquid is different.
flow.kid: Help put a label on each glass. Pour 3 spoons into each one.
flow.parent: Wash the shell in water first, so no egg is left on it. Keep the thin skin on the inside of the shell. That is fine. If you use cowrie shells or seashells, use one small shell in each glass.

flow.context: In this step you drop the shells in and watch closely.
flow.do: 1. Drop one piece of shell into each glass, one after the other, quickly. 2. Shine the torch through the side of each glass. 3. Watch each glass for about a minute.
flow.say: Watch the shell closely. Do you see anything coming off it?
flow.kid: Drop a shell in each glass. Shine the torch from the side. Look closely.
flow.parent: In vinegar, tiny bubbles appear on the shell within a minute. The piece may float up. Lemon juice usually gives fewer, smaller bubbles, so look closely. Water, milk and sugar water show no new bubbles. A few air bubbles may stick to any shell at the very start. They do not keep coming.

check.q: Which glass had the most bubbles on the shell?
check.why: Vinegar has an acid in it. The acid breaks down the shell, and a gas comes out as bubbles. If you picked sugar water, look again: sugar water does not make bubbles on the shell.

flow.context: In this step you write down what you saw in each glass.
flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they saw in each glass. 2. Write 'lots', 'a few' or 'none' for the bubbles. 3. Let them draw each glass.
flow.say: Tell me about each glass. Lots of bubbles, a few, or none?
flow.kid: Say what you saw in each glass. Draw the bubbles.

ask.q: Was your guess right for the sugar water?
good: No, the sugar water did nothing to the shell.
Yes, I guessed it would do nothing.

flow.context: In this step you leave the shells in their glasses overnight.
flow.do: 1. Cover the glasses with a plate or a piece of cardboard. 2. Put them where no one will knock them over. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Tomorrow we will feel each piece. What do you think the shell in vinegar will feel like? Why?
flow.kid: Cover the glasses. What will the vinegar shell feel like tomorrow? Why?
flow.parent: Keep the glasses away from small children and pets. The vinegar may smell a little. That is normal.

flow.wait: Leave the glasses until the same time tomorrow.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the eggshell test. You take out each piece of shell and feel it.
flow.do: 1. Lift each piece out with a teaspoon. 2. Rinse it under the tap. 3. Let your child press it gently between two fingers. 4. Write 'hard' or 'soft and bendy' in the table.
flow.say: Press each piece gently. Is it still hard? Or is it soft and bendy?
flow.kid: Rinse each piece. Press it gently. Is it hard, or soft?
flow.parent: The vinegar piece is usually soft and bendy, or partly gone, with only the thin skin left. The lemon piece may be a little soft at the edges. The others stay hard. Sugar water may smell a little. The shell in it stays hard.

flow.context: This is the last step of the eggshell test. You say what you think now, what you saw, and why.
flow.do: 1. Ask the three questions below, one at a time. 2. Write the answers down.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see that tells you so? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: What do you think now? What did you see? Why?

good: Sour things like vinegar and lemon harm a hard shell.
Sugar water did not harm the shell.
The vinegar shell made bubbles and went soft. The sugar water shell stayed hard.

ask.q: Why do you think it happened?
good: Vinegar has acid in it, and acid wears away the shell.
Sour things have something in them that breaks the shell.

flow.think: Your teeth are harder than eggshell. A tooth is never left in vinegar for a day. So when could acid touch your teeth?

experiments.title: The Root Test: why does a milk tooth wobble?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a pretend gum from atta dough. You push two pencils into it as pretend teeth: one deep, with a long root, and one shallow, with a short root. Then you push each one gently from the side and count how many pushes it takes to fall over.
experiments.question: Does a tooth with a long root stand firmer than a tooth with a short root?
experiments.predict: Look at the two pencils. Which one will fall over first when you push it? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both pencils are the same kind and the same length. They go in the same block of dough. Each push is the same: one finger, a gentle tap at the top of the pencil, from the same side. We do each pencil three times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: atta dough, made from about 2 cups of atta and some water, kneaded firm
2 pencils of the same length, or 2 used pencils cut to the same length by a grown-up
a ruler with centimetres
a steel plate or tray

schedule.what: Make the dough gum. Push in two pencils, one deep and one shallow. Push each from the side and count. Do it three times. Say what you found.

experiments.record: Write your guess and reason. Fill in the table. Draw the two pencils in the dough, showing how deep each one went.

setup.art: A thick round block of atta dough, about as tall as a hand is wide, on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. Make a thick, firm block of dough. This is the gum.

setup.art: Two pencils standing in the dough: one pushed in deep, one only a little way, with a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Push one pencil in 4 cm deep and one only 1 cm deep.

setup.art: A child's finger tapping the top of the short-root pencil from the side, and the pencil tipping over.
setup.caption: 3. Tap each one gently from the side. Count the taps until it falls.

flow.context: This is the first step of the root test. You look at two pretend teeth and guess which will fall first.
flow.do: 1. Show your child the two pencils and the dough. 2. Explain that the dough is the gum and the pencils are teeth. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: One tooth will have a long root, deep in the gum. One will have a short root. Which will fall over first? Why?
flow.kid: One tooth has a long root. One has a short root. Which falls first? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will fall first?
good: The short one, because it is not held in much.
The long one, because more of it sticks out.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is good. Write it down.

flow.context: In this step you make the pretend gum and put in the pretend teeth.
flow.do: 1. Knead the dough until firm, and press it into a thick block on the plate, about 6 cm tall. 2. Mark 4 cm on one pencil and 1 cm on the other with a pen. 3. Push each pencil in, point first, up to its mark, about 5 cm apart.
flow.say: This pencil has a long root, like an adult tooth. This one has a short root, like a milk tooth whose root has been taken away.
flow.kid: Help knead the dough. Push in one pencil deep. Push in one only a little.
flow.parent: Firm dough works best. Soft, sticky dough lets both pencils flop. Add a little more atta if it sticks to your fingers.

flow.context: In this step you push each pretend tooth and count.
flow.do: 1. Your child taps the top of the short-root pencil gently from the side, counting each tap aloud. 2. Stop when it falls over or leans flat. 3. Do the same with the long-root pencil. 4. Push both back to their marks and do it twice more. 5. Write each count in the table.
flow.say: Same gentle tap each time, from the same side. We do it three times, because one try can be a fluke.
flow.kid: Tap the top gently, from the side. Count each tap. Stop when it falls.
flow.parent: The short-root pencil usually falls in one or two taps. The long-root pencil usually stands for many taps, and may only lean. Keep the taps gentle, the same each time.

check.q: Which pretend tooth fell over with fewer taps?
options: The one with the long root
The one with the short root
They fell with the same number of taps
check.why: A short root has only a little dough holding it, so it tips easily. If you picked the long root, look at your table again. A milk tooth wobbles for the same reason: its root has been taken away.

flow.context: This is the last step of the root test. You say what you think now, what you saw, and why.
flow.do: 1. Ask the three questions below. 2. Write the answers down.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why does a milk tooth wobble before it falls out?
flow.kid: What do you think now? What did you see? Why does a milk tooth wobble?

ask.q: Why does a milk tooth wobble before it falls out?
good: Its root gets short, so the gum cannot hold it tight.
The body takes the root away, like our short pencil.

activities.title: Torch Tour: your teeth and a grown-up's teeth
activities.context: In this activity you look at your own teeth with a torch and a mirror, and feel them with your tongue. Then you look at a grown-up's teeth and find the teeth they have that you do not have yet.

materials.item: a torch, or the light on a phone
a mirror
a grown-up who is happy to open wide
paper and four colour pencils: blue, yellow, orange and green

schedule.what: Feel your teeth with your tongue, front to back. Look with a torch. Look at a grown-up's teeth. Find their premolars. Draw both.

activities.record: Draw one side of your top teeth and one side of a grown-up's top teeth. Colour incisors blue, canines yellow, premolars orange and molars green.

setup.art: A child with the tip of their tongue touching the edge of a front tooth, eyes looking up as if thinking.
setup.caption: 1. Feel your teeth with your tongue, from the front to the back.

setup.art: A child at a mirror, pulling one cheek back with a finger, while a grown-up shines a torch into the mouth.
setup.caption: 2. Look at your teeth with a torch.

setup.art: A child shining a torch into a grown-up's open mouth, pointing at the two teeth just behind the pointed canine.
setup.caption: 3. Find the grown-up's premolars.

flow.context: This is the first step of the torch tour. You feel your own teeth with your tongue.
flow.do: 1. Ask your child to close their eyes. 2. Ask them to slide their tongue along their top teeth, from the middle to the back. 3. Ask them how the teeth change.
flow.say: Close your eyes. Slide your tongue from your front teeth to your back teeth. How do they change as you go?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Slide your tongue from the front teeth to the back. How do they change?

ask.q: How do your teeth feel as you go back?
good: The front ones are thin and flat, with a sharp edge.
Then there is a pointy one.
The back ones are wide and bumpy.

flow.parent: Wash your hands, and let your child wash theirs, before anyone touches a mouth.

flow.context: In this step you look at your own teeth with a torch.
flow.do: 1. Hold the torch while your child looks in the mirror. 2. Ask them to find the incisors, the pointed canine, and the wide back molars. 3. Count the back teeth behind the canine on one side, top row.
flow.say: Find your thin front teeth, your pointed tooth, and your wide back teeth. How many wide teeth are behind the pointed one?
flow.kid: Find the thin front teeth, the pointed one and the wide back ones. Count the back ones.
flow.parent: Most children of 7 have 2 milk molars behind the canine on each side. Many also have a third, bigger one at the back. That is the first adult molar.

flow.context: In this step you look at a grown-up's teeth and compare.
flow.do: 1. A grown-up opens wide. 2. Your child shines the torch. 3. Help them find the canine, then the next two teeth behind it. These are the premolars. 4. Count all the teeth behind the canine on one side.
flow.say: Behind the pointed tooth, a grown-up has two teeth with two little points on top. These are premolars. Do you have them?
flow.kid: Look in the grown-up's mouth. Find the pointed tooth. Look at the next two teeth. These are premolars.

ask.q: What is different about the grown-up's back teeth?
good: There are more of them.
They have premolars, and I don't.
Their teeth are bigger and a bit more yellow.

flow.parent: A grown-up usually has 2 premolars and 2 or 3 molars behind the canine on each side. Some grown-ups have had teeth taken out or filled. That is fine to point out.

flow.context: This is the last step of the torch tour. You draw what you saw.
flow.do: 1. Your child draws one side of their top teeth, and one side of the grown-up's. 2. They colour each kind of tooth.
flow.say: Draw one side of your teeth and one side of mine. Colour incisors blue, canines yellow, premolars orange and molars green.
flow.kid: Draw your teeth and the grown-up's teeth. Colour each kind.

activities.title: A Tooth in Layers: make one from dough
activities.context: In this activity you make a big model tooth from three colours of atta dough: white enamel outside, yellow dentine under it, and red pulp in the middle. Then a grown-up cuts it in half so you can see the layers.

materials.item: atta dough, about 1 cup, split into three balls
a pinch of turmeric, to colour one ball yellow
a spoon of beetroot juice, or a drop of red food colour, to colour one ball red
a little extra dry atta or maida, to keep the white ball pale
a butter knife and a plate

activities.safety: A grown-up does the cutting. Turmeric and beetroot can stain clothes, so wear an old shirt.

schedule.what: Colour three dough balls. Wrap red inside yellow, and yellow inside white. Shape a tooth with roots. Cut it in half and name the layers.

activities.record: Draw your cut tooth and label the enamel, dentine, pulp and root.

setup.art: Three balls of dough on a plate: one pale white, one turmeric yellow, one beetroot red.
setup.caption: 1. Make three colours of dough.

setup.art: Hands wrapping a small red ball inside a yellow layer, then inside a thin white layer.
setup.caption: 2. Wrap red in yellow, and yellow in a thin white skin on top.

setup.art: A dough tooth cut in half on a plate, showing a red middle, a yellow layer and a thin white top layer, with two roots.
setup.caption: 3. Cut it in half. Name each layer.

flow.context: This is the first step of the dough tooth. You make three colours of dough.
flow.do: 1. Split the dough into three balls: one large, one middle-sized, one small. 2. Knead turmeric into the large ball until it is yellow. 3. Knead beetroot juice into the small ball until it is red. 4. Dust the middle ball with dry atta to keep it pale.
flow.say: The red is the pulp, the living middle. The yellow is dentine. The white is enamel, the hard outside.
flow.kid: Knead the colours in. Red is pulp. Yellow is dentine. White is enamel.
flow.parent: If the red dough gets sticky, add a pinch of dry atta.

flow.context: In this step you build the tooth.
flow.do: 1. Roll the red ball into a short sausage. 2. Wrap the yellow dough all round it, and pull two legs down for roots. 3. Flatten the white dough thin and lay it over the top part only. 4. Press little hills on top, like a molar.
flow.say: Enamel covers only the top, the part above the gum. The roots are under the gum, so they have no enamel.
flow.kid: Wrap the yellow round the red. Make two roots. Put white only on the top.

ask.q: Why does the white only go on the top?
good: Because enamel covers the part we bite with.
The roots are in the gum, so they don't need it.

flow.context: This is the last step of the dough tooth. You cut it and look inside.
flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts the tooth from top to bottom with the butter knife. 2. Your child names each layer. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Point to the enamel, the dentine and the pulp. If acid wore a hole through the white, what would it reach next?
flow.kid: Name each layer. If acid made a hole in the white, what is next?

ask.q: If acid wore a hole through the enamel, what would it reach next?
good: The dentine, the yellow part.
Then the pulp, and that would hurt.

activities.title: Sweet and Sour Tally: how many acid times in a day?
activities.context: In this activity you keep a tally for one day. Every time you eat or drink something sweet or sour, you make a mark. At the end of the day you count how many acid times your teeth had.

materials.item: a sheet of paper with two columns: 'Sweet' and 'Sour'
a pencil, kept somewhere easy to reach, like the fridge door

schedule.what: Through the day, make a mark each time you eat or drink something sweet or sour. In the evening, count the marks and talk about them.

activities.record: Keep the tally sheet. At the bottom, write the total, and one change that would give fewer acid times.

setup.art: A tally sheet stuck to a fridge door with two columns, Sweet and Sour, and a pencil tied on a string.
setup.caption: 1. Stick a tally sheet on the fridge.

setup.art: A child making a tally mark after eating a sweet biscuit, with a glass of lemon juice on the table.
setup.caption: 2. Make a mark each time you eat or drink something sweet or sour.

setup.art: A child counting groups of five tally marks in the evening with a grown-up.
setup.caption: 3. In the evening, count the marks.

flow.context: This is the first step of the tally. You get the sheet ready in the morning.
flow.do: 1. Draw two columns on the sheet: Sweet and Sour. 2. Stick it on the fridge with the pencil. 3. Explain the rule below.
flow.say: Each time you eat or drink something sweet or sour today, make one mark. Tea with sugar counts. A sweet counts. Lemon rice counts as sour.
flow.kid: Each time you eat something sweet or sour, make a mark.
flow.parent: Count each time, not each bite. One biscuit after school is one mark. Three biscuits at different times are three marks.

flow.context: In this step you keep the tally going all day.
flow.do: Remind your child to make a mark after each sweet or sour snack, drink or meal.
flow.say: Did that have sugar in it, or was it sour? Make a mark.
flow.kid: Was that sweet or sour? Make a mark.

flow.context: This is the last step of the tally. You count the marks in the evening.
flow.do: 1. Count the marks in each column with your child. 2. Add them up. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Each mark was a time when acid could work on your teeth. How many were there? Which ones could we move to mealtimes?
flow.kid: Count your marks. Each one is an acid time. Which could happen at a meal instead?

ask.q: How could you have fewer acid times tomorrow?
good: Eat the sweet with lunch, not later.
Drink water instead of juice between meals.
Not sip a sweet drink slowly all afternoon.

flow.parent: This is not about being good or bad. It is about noticing. A meal with a sweet in it is one acid time. Sipping a sweet drink slowly for an hour keeps acid on the teeth the whole hour.

activities.title: Gap Watch: a new tooth coming in (if you have a wobbly tooth or a gap)
activities.context: If you have a wobbly tooth or a gap where a milk tooth fell out, this activity is for you. For one week, you look at the gap every day with a torch and a mirror, and draw what you see.

materials.item: a torch and a mirror
a notebook with 7 small boxes drawn on one page, one for each day

schedule.what: Look at the gap or wobbly tooth. Draw it in box 1.
Look and draw in box 7. Compare day 1 and day 7.

activities.record: Seven drawings of the same gap, one for each day. On day 7, write one change you saw.

setup.art: A child at a mirror pulling their lip down to show a gap, with a torch shining in.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the gap with a torch.

setup.art: A notebook page with seven small boxes, each with a drawing of a gap, and a white edge slowly getting bigger.
setup.caption: 2. Draw it in one box each day.

flow.context: This is the first day of the gap watch.
flow.do: 1. Hold the torch while your child looks at the gap in the mirror. 2. Ask what they can see. 3. They draw it in box 1.
flow.say: Look in the gap. Can you see the edge of a new tooth? Draw just what you see today.
flow.kid: Look in the gap. Can you see a new tooth? Draw it.
flow.parent: A new tooth can take a few weeks to come up fully. In a week you may see only a little change. That is normal.

flow.wait: Look again each day for the next 6 days.
flow.context: This is the daily look for the gap watch.
flow.do: 1. Look at the gap again with the torch. 2. Your child draws it in the next box.
flow.say: Has anything changed since yesterday?
flow.kid: Look again. Draw it in the next box. Did it change?

flow.context: This is the last day of the gap watch.
flow.do: 1. Compare box 1 and box 7. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at your first drawing and your last drawing. What changed? Where was the new tooth before?
flow.kid: Look at your first and last drawings. What changed?

ask.q: Where was the new tooth before you could see it?
good: Inside my jaw, under the gum.
Under the milk tooth.

activities.title: Twig Brush: try a datun (if you can get a neem or babool twig)
activities.context: If you can get a fresh neem or babool twig from a market or a tree, this activity lets you try the twig toothbrush that people in India have used for a very long time. It is called a datun. You chew one end until it goes soft and bristly, then clean your teeth with it.

materials.item: a fresh neem or babool twig, about as thick as a pencil and as long as your hand, washed. Some markets and shops sell them
a mirror and a glass of water

activities.safety: A grown-up checks the twig is neem or babool, from a clean place, and washes it first. Spit out the bits. Do not swallow the twig.

schedule.what: Chew one end of the twig until it is soft. Gently clean your teeth with it. Compare it with your toothbrush.

activities.record: Draw the chewed end of the twig next to your toothbrush. Write one thing the twig did well and one thing the brush did better.

setup.art: A washed neem twig the length of a hand, with one end chewed into soft bristles.
setup.caption: 1. Chew one end until it is soft and bristly.

setup.art: A child at a mirror rubbing the soft end of a twig gently on the front teeth.
setup.caption: 2. Rub it gently on your teeth.

flow.context: This is the first step of the twig brush. You make the bristles.
flow.do: 1. Wash the twig. 2. Your child chews one end gently for a few minutes, until the end splits into soft threads. 3. They spit out any bits.
flow.say: Chew the end gently. It will go soft and split into tiny bristles. Neem tastes bitter.
flow.kid: Chew the end gently. It goes soft. Neem tastes bitter. Spit out the bits.

flow.context: In this step you clean your teeth with the twig.
flow.do: 1. Your child rubs the soft end gently on the front teeth, then tries the back teeth. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Clean your front teeth, then try the back ones. Is it easy to reach the back?
flow.kid: Clean your front teeth. Then try the back. Is it easy?

ask.q: What did the twig do well? What was hard?
good: It cleaned the front teeth well.
It was hard to reach the back teeth.
It tasted bitter.

flow.context: This is the last step of the twig brush. You compare it with a toothbrush.
flow.do: Ask your child to compare the twig and the brush.
flow.say: A toothbrush has a small head that reaches the back. Toothpaste has fluoride. A twig needs no factory. Which would you choose, and when?
flow.kid: Which would you choose: the twig or the brush? Why?
flow.parent: Scientists still compare how well twigs and brushes clean. Brushing with fluoride toothpaste is what dentists in India advise for children.

projects.title: The Family Tooth Book
projects.context: In this 3-day project you ask people in your family about their milk teeth. When did their first one fall out? What did they do with it? You make a small book of their answers.

materials.item: 4 sheets of paper folded in half and stapled into a small book
pencils and colours
a phone, to call a grandparent or relative who lives far away, if you like

schedule.what: Make the book. Ask two people the three questions. Write or draw their answers.
Ask two more people, in person or on the phone.
Draw a cover. Count how many people lost their first tooth at 5, 6, 7 or 8. Show the book to the family.

projects.record: The finished book, with one page for each person and a counting page at the end.

setup.art: Four sheets of paper folded and stapled into a small book, with 'Our Family's Teeth' written on the cover.
setup.caption: 1. Make a small book.

setup.art: A girl holding the book and asking her grandmother a question, with the grandmother smiling and pointing to her own teeth.
setup.caption: 2. Ask each person the three questions.

setup.art: A page with a tally of ages 5, 6, 7 and 8, and small drawings of teeth.
setup.caption: 3. Count how old each person was.

flow.context: This is day 1 of the family tooth book.
flow.do: 1. Fold and staple the book. 2. Write the three questions at the front. 3. Your child asks two family members and writes or draws the answers.
flow.say: Ask: How old were you when your first milk tooth fell out? Which tooth was it? What did you do with it?
flow.kid: Ask: How old were you? Which tooth fell first? What did you do with it?
flow.parent: Help write the answers if needed. Many families in India have tooth customs, like throwing the tooth on a roof or burying it. Write down whatever people say.

flow.context: This is day 2 of the family tooth book.
flow.do: Your child asks two more people. A phone call to a grandparent or an aunt works well.
flow.say: Who else could we ask? Maybe Paati, or your aunt in Kolkata?
flow.kid: Ask two more people. You can call someone on the phone.

flow.context: This is day 3 of the family tooth book.
flow.do: 1. Your child draws a cover. 2. On the last page, they make a tally of the ages: 5, 6, 7, 8 or more. 3. They show the book to the family.
flow.say: At what age did most people lose their first tooth? Did anyone do something unusual with their tooth?
flow.kid: Count the ages. Which age came up most? Show your book.

ask.q: What did most people do with their tooth?
good: Threw it on the roof.
Kept it in a box.
Lost it, nobody remembers.

challenges.title: Pack a Tooth-Kind Tiffin
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You plan a school tiffin and a drink that are tasty and filling, and give your teeth as few acid times as you can.
challenges.problem: Plan a tiffin for one school day. It must be tasty, it must fill you up until home time, and it must give your teeth only one acid time or none.
constraints: Use only food your family really has or cooks.
At most one sweet or sour thing, eaten with the rest of the tiffin.
Include one crunchy vegetable or fruit.
The drink must not be sweet.
materials: a tiffin box, to check what fits
the tally sheet from the sweet and sour tally, if you made one
general: Idli with coconut chutney, cucumber sticks, and water.
Lemon rice, carrot sticks, and water.
Roti with dal, a guava, and water.
creative: A small bag of roasted chana and peanuts to chew last, which makes plenty of saliva.
Putting the one sweet thing in the same box as the meal, so it is eaten with the meal, not later.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your tiffin plan. Show it to the family cook and ask if it can be made. Then eat it one day, and say if it kept you full.

setup.art: An open steel tiffin box with three sections, and a child drawing a plan beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your plan for each section of the tiffin.

setup.art: A child showing the drawing to a woman in the kitchen, who is pointing to the cucumber.
setup.caption: 2. Ask the family cook if it can be made.

flow.context: This is the first step of the tiffin challenge. You read the problem.
flow.do: 1. Read the problem and the rules aloud. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Your tiffin must be tasty and filling, but give your teeth only one acid time at most. What will you put in?
flow.kid: Plan a tiffin. Tasty, filling, and only one acid time. What will you put in?

ask.q: What counts as an acid time?
good: Something sweet, because bacteria make acid from sugar.
Something sour, like lemon or raw mango.

flow.context: In this step you draw your plan.
flow.do: Let your child draw the tiffin. Help them check each rule.
flow.say: Check each rule. Is there one crunchy thing? Is the drink not sweet?
flow.kid: Draw your tiffin. Check each rule.
flow.parent: There are many good answers. Let your child choose real food your family eats.

flow.context: This is the last step of the tiffin challenge.
flow.do: 1. Your child shows the plan to the family cook. 2. Agree on a day to make it.
flow.say: Tell us why each thing is in your tiffin.
flow.kid: Say why you chose each thing.

videos.title: How milk teeth fall out and adult teeth come in: an animation or X-ray view
videos.why: Shows adult teeth already in the jaw under the milk teeth, which a child cannot see.
videos.check: Find a real, accurate video for age 7. Check it shows adult teeth forming under the milk teeth and the milk tooth root being taken away, not snapping off.

videos.title: Eggshell in vinegar, filmed close up or sped up
videos.why: Shows the bubbles and the shell going soft over a day, to compare with the child's own test.
videos.check: Find a real video. Check it does not claim eggshell is the same material as tooth enamel.

videos.title: How to brush teeth, for children, from a dental school or health service
videos.why: Shows gentle brushing of every surface, including the back molars, with a pea-sized blob of fluoride toothpaste.
videos.check: Find a real video from a dental school, dental association or health service. Check it says brush gently, twice a day, about two minutes, and spit out.

quiz.p: How many milk teeth does a child usually have when they are all in?
quiz.why: A child has 20 milk teeth. 32 is the most a grown-up can have. Picking 32 mixes up milk teeth and adult teeth.

quiz.p: Where are your adult teeth before they come out?
opts: Inside the jaw, under the milk teeth
Nowhere yet: they start growing when a milk tooth falls
quiz.why: Adult teeth form inside the jaw years before they come out. Picking 'nowhere yet' is a common guess. X-ray pictures show they are already there.

quiz.p: Why does a milk tooth get wobbly before it falls out?
opts: The body takes its root away as the adult tooth comes up
The child pushes it with their tongue
quiz.why: The root is dissolved bit by bit, so the tooth is held only weakly. Pushing with the tongue does not make a firm tooth wobble.
quiz.context: This question is about the root test. You push two pencils into a block of atta dough, one deep and one shallow, and see which one falls over first.

quiz.p: Which teeth bite a piece off a guava?
quiz.why: Incisors are the thin, flat front teeth that bite and cut. Molars grind food at the back.

quiz.p: What is the job of the wide, bumpy molars?
opts: To grind food into a paste
To hold the tongue in place
quiz.why: Molars grind food. Biting a piece off is the job of incisors.

quiz.p: Which part of a tooth is alive, with blood vessels and nerves?
quiz.why: The pulp is the living middle. Enamel is hard mineral on the outside. Plaque is the sticky layer of bacteria on top of a tooth.

quiz.p: Which is the hardest material in your body?
quiz.why: Enamel is harder than bone. Many people guess bone.

quiz.p: In the eggshell test, which pair of liquids made bubbles on the shell?
quiz.why: Lemon juice and vinegar are sour, because they have acids in them. Acid breaks down the shell. Sugar water and milk did not make bubbles.
quiz.context: This question is about the eggshell test. You drop pieces of eggshell into water, sugar water, milk, lemon juice and vinegar, watch for bubbles, and feel the pieces again the next day.

quiz.p: Sugar water did not harm the eggshell. So how does sugar harm teeth?
opts: Bacteria in plaque eat the sugar and make acid
Sugar is very hard and scratches teeth
Sugar does not harm teeth at all
quiz.why: Bacteria living in plaque eat sugar and make acid right on the tooth. Picking 'does not harm teeth at all' misses the bacteria.
quiz.context: This question is about the eggshell test. You drop pieces of eggshell into water, sugar water, milk, lemon juice and vinegar, watch for bubbles, and feel the pieces again the next day.

quiz.p: What does the fluoride in toothpaste do?
opts: It makes enamel harder for acid to wear away
It makes teeth whiter by painting them
quiz.why: A little fluoride makes enamel harder for acid to dissolve. It does not make teeth grow back.

quiz.p: How much toothpaste should a child of 7 put on the brush?
opts: A blob about the size of a pea
The whole length of the brush
quiz.why: A pea-sized blob of fluoride toothpaste is enough. Too much fluoride swallowed while teeth are growing can spot them.

quiz.p: Anjali, a girl in Class 2, guessed that sugar water would harm the eggshell. It did not. What should she do now?
opts: Change her idea to fit what the test showed
quiz.why: A guess is there to be tested. When the test shows something else, a scientist changes the idea. Guessing wrong is part of finding out.
quiz.context: This question is about the eggshell test. You drop pieces of eggshell into water, sugar water, milk, lemon juice and vinegar, watch for bubbles, and feel the pieces again the next day.

items.p: Draw a line from each kind of tooth to its job.
items.why: Front teeth are thin and sharp for cutting. Pointed canines grip. Wide, bumpy back teeth grind.

items.p: A child has ____ milk teeth.
items.why: All 20 milk teeth are usually in by about age 3. A grown-up can have up to 32 adult teeth.

items.p: In the eggshell test, which liquid made the shell go soft and bendy by the next day?
items.why: Vinegar has an acid in it, which breaks down the shell. Water and milk left it hard. Picking milk may mean thinking any drink harms a shell. The test showed it does not.
items.context: This question is about the eggshell test. You drop pieces of eggshell into water, sugar water, milk, lemon juice and vinegar, watch for bubbles, and feel the pieces again the next day.

items.p: In the eggshell test, the sugar water made the shell fizz.
items.why: False. Sugar water did not fizz on the shell. Sugar harms teeth only when bacteria in plaque eat sugar and make acid.
items.context: This question is about the eggshell test. You drop pieces of eggshell into water, sugar water, milk, lemon juice and vinegar, watch for bubbles, and feel the pieces again the next day.

items.p: Draw the glass of vinegar with the eggshell in it, just after you dropped the shell in.
items.a: A glass of liquid with a piece of shell, and small bubbles on the shell and rising up.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the bubbles coming from the shell itself. They show the acid was breaking the shell down.
items.context: This question is about the eggshell test. You drop pieces of eggshell into water, sugar water, milk, lemon juice and vinegar, watch for bubbles, and feel the pieces again the next day.
items.art: An empty outline of a glass for the child to draw in.

items.p: Label the parts of this tooth: enamel, dentine, pulp, root.
a: the yellow layer under it: dentine
the part in the jaw: root
items.why: Enamel is the hard outside. Dentine is under it. The living pulp is in the middle. The root holds the tooth in the jaw.
items.art: A tooth cut in half from top to bottom, with four empty label lines pointing to the outer layer, the middle layer, the centre and the root.

items.p: Sowmya, a girl in Class 2, had 20 milk teeth. 3 have fallen out. How many milk teeth does she have now?
items.why: 20 take away 3 is 17. Count back from 20: 19, 18, 17.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why does a fallen milk tooth have almost no root?
items.a: The adult tooth growing under it made the body take the root away, bit by bit, to make room.
items.why: A strong answer says the root was taken away, or dissolved, not broken off, because the adult tooth was coming up underneath.

items.p: Sort these into 'helps teeth' and 'acid time'.
items: a glass of water after lunch
items.why: Sweet and sour things give acid times. Brushing, water and the dentist help.

items.p: Three of these are sour. Which one is not?
items.why: Cucumber is not sour. Tamarind, lemon and raw mango taste sour because they have acids in them.

items.p: Meenakshi and her brother Kiran are talking about milk teeth.

views.says: I don't need to brush my milk teeth much. They are going to fall out anyway.
You must brush them. You will use them for years, and a hole in one can hurt.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Meenakshi, because milk teeth are used for chewing and speaking for many years, a cavity can hurt, and milk teeth hold the space for adult teeth. It also says Kiran is right that milk teeth do fall out.
items.why: Kiran is right that they fall out. Meenakshi is right that they still matter while they are there.

items.p: Put the steps of the eggshell test in order.
items: Guess which liquids will harm the shell, and say why
Pour the same amount of each liquid into its glass
Drop in the pieces of shell and watch for bubbles
Leave them until the next day
Rinse each piece and press it
items.why: We guess first, so the test can check our guess. We use the same amount of each liquid, so only the liquid is different.
items.context: This question is about the eggshell test. You drop pieces of eggshell into water, sugar water, milk, lemon juice and vinegar, watch for bubbles, and feel the pieces again the next day.

items.p: In the root test, the pencil pushed in only 1 cm fell over after 1 tap. What does that show about a milk tooth?
opts: A tooth with a short root is held weakly, so it wobbles
Pencils are not like teeth at all
A long root makes a tooth fall out
items.why: A short root has only a little gum around it to hold it. A milk tooth's root is taken away before it falls, so it wobbles. Picking 'a long root makes a tooth fall out' is the opposite of what the test showed.
items.context: This question is about the root test. You push two pencils into a block of atta dough, one deep and one shallow, and see which one falls over first.

items.p: Why does a grown-up have premolars, but a child of 7 does not?
opts: Premolars grow in when the back milk teeth fall out
Children eat no food that needs crushing
items.why: When a child's back milk molars fall out, between about age 10 and 12, premolars grow in their place.

items.p: In the eggshell test, why did we put one piece of shell in plain water?
items.a: So we could see what happens with nothing sour or sweet added. If the water shell stays hard, we know the vinegar caused the change.
items.why: A strong answer says the water glass is for comparing. Without it, we could not tell if any wet shell goes soft.
items.context: This question is about the eggshell test. You drop pieces of eggshell into water, sugar water, milk, lemon juice and vinegar, watch for bubbles, and feel the pieces again the next day.

items.p: If acid wears a deep hole in your enamel, the enamel grows back by itself.
items.why: False. The cells that made the enamel are gone once a tooth comes through the gum. Saliva and fluoride can only repair the very first soft spot. A deep hole needs a dentist.

items.p: Draw the two pencils in the dough from the root test. Show how deep each one went.
items.a: A block of dough with one pencil deep in it and one only a little way in.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the long root deep in the dough, like an adult tooth, and the short root near the top, like a milk tooth before it falls.
items.context: This question is about the root test. You push two pencils into a block of atta dough, one deep and one shallow, and see which one falls over first.
items.art: An empty box with a dough block drawn at the bottom.

items.p: The hard, white outside layer of a tooth is called ____.
items.why: Enamel is the hardest material in the human body.

items.p: Farzana and her grandmother are cleaning their teeth.

views.says: I have cleaned my teeth with a neem twig every morning of my life. It needs no shop and no plastic.
I use a toothbrush with fluoride toothpaste. The small head reaches my back teeth, and the fluoride makes enamel harder for acid.

items.ask: Which way would you choose? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives a reason, such as 'the brush reaches the back teeth' or 'the twig needs no plastic'. It also says what the other is right about.
items.why: Both have good points. Scientists still compare how well twigs and brushes clean. Fluoride is a strong reason to use toothpaste.

items.p: Shalini, a girl in Class 2, kept a sweet and sour tally for one day. She had 3 sweet marks and 2 sour marks. How many acid times did her teeth have?
items.why: 3 add 2 is 5. Each mark is one time when acid could work on her teeth.

items.p: Sort these teeth into 'a child of 7 has them' and 'only grown-ups have them'.
items.why: Children have incisors, canines and molars. Premolars come in at about 10 to 12. Wisdom teeth come in at about 17 to 25, or never.

items.p: Label the kinds of teeth on this picture of a grown-up's top teeth: incisor, canine, premolar, molar.
a: tooth with two points behind it: premolar
items.why: From the front: incisors, then the canine, then two premolars, then the molars.
items.art: A curved row of a grown-up's top teeth seen from below, with four empty label lines pointing to a front tooth, a pointed tooth, a two-pointed tooth and a wide back tooth.

items.p: Tamarind water tastes very sour. If you put a piece of eggshell in it, what do you think would happen? Why?
items.a: It would probably make bubbles on the shell and soften it, because sour things have acid in them, like vinegar and lemon.
items.why: A strong answer uses the eggshell test as evidence: sour liquids made the shell fizz. It may also say how to check: try it.
items.context: This question is about the eggshell test. You drop pieces of eggshell into water, sugar water, milk, lemon juice and vinegar, watch for bubbles, and feel the pieces again the next day.

items.p: Nisha, a girl in Class 3, says: 'My teeth are harder than eggshell, so lemon juice can never harm them.' What is wrong with her thinking?
items.a: Being hard does not stop acid. Enamel is harder than eggshell, but it has calcium in it too, and acid can slowly dissolve it.
items.why: A strong answer says hardness protects against breaking, not against acid. Many sips of something sour give acid many chances.

items.p: Dr Revathi and Dr Usha are two dentists. They disagree about brushing after a sour drink.

views.says: Wait for a while after a sour drink. The enamel is a little softer just after, so brushing at once may wear it.
Brushing soon after does very little harm, especially with fluoride toothpaste. What matters most is brushing every day.

items.ask: Which dentist do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say what the other dentist has right. What test would help them decide?
items.a: A strong answer picks one with a reason, says something fair about the other, and suggests a test, such as comparing teeth of people who wait and people who don't.
items.why: Scientists still argue about this. Both agree that brushing every day with fluoride toothpaste helps.

items.p: Which of these gives teeth the longest acid time?
opts: A sweet drink sipped slowly for an hour
items.why: Sipping slowly keeps sugar and acid in the mouth for the whole hour. One sweet with a meal is one short acid time. Water gives none.

items.p: In some villages, the well water has a lot of fluoride in it. What can happen to children's teeth there?
opts: Their teeth grow with brown or white spots
Their teeth never get cavities at all
Their milk teeth never fall out
items.why: Too much fluoride while teeth are forming spots the enamel. This is called dental fluorosis. It is common in parts of Nalgonda in Telangana and in Rajasthan.

items.p: Brushing very hard cleans teeth better than brushing gently.
items.why: False. Plaque is soft and comes off with gentle brushing. Hard brushing can hurt the gums.

items.p: Design a toothbrush that makes it easy to clean the very back molars. Draw it, and label one thing that makes it good.
items.a: Any design with a reason, such as a small head, a bent neck or soft bristles.
items.why: A strong design shows a way to reach behind the last molar and into its grooves, and says why.

items.p: Put these in order, from youngest age to oldest.
items: The first milk teeth come through the gums
The first adult molars come in at the back
The front milk teeth fall out
items.why: First milk teeth at about 6 months. All 20 by about 3. First adult molars and front teeth change at about 6 to 7. Wisdom teeth at about 17 to 25, if at all.

items.p: A grown-up has 32 teeth. 4 of them are wisdom teeth still hidden in the jaw. How many teeth can you see?
items.why: 32 take away 4 is 28. Many grown-ups have 28 teeth you can see.

items.p: Three of these help teeth after a snack. Which one does not?
items.why: A sweet cola has sugar for the bacteria. The cola is also sour, with acid in the drink itself. The others rinse, make saliva or remove plaque.

items.p: Why did the shell in vinegar make bubbles? Say what was happening to the shell.
items.a: The acid in the vinegar was breaking down the shell. As the shell broke down, a gas came out as bubbles.
items.why: A strong answer says the bubbles came from the shell, as the acid broke it down. That is also why the shell went soft by the next day.
items.context: This question is about the eggshell test. You drop pieces of eggshell into water, sugar water, milk, lemon juice and vinegar, watch for bubbles, and feel the pieces again the next day.

applications: Dentists fill cavities, because a deep hole in enamel does not grow back.
Most toothpaste has a little fluoride in it, to make enamel harder for acid to wear.
Some towns and cities in the world add a little fluoride to tap water. In parts of India with too much fluoride in the ground water, water is treated to take some out.
Dentists use X-ray pictures to see adult teeth growing inside a child's jaw.
Scientists who study bones and teeth can tell roughly how old a child was from which teeth were in the jaw.

open_questions.q: How does the body know exactly when to start taking away a milk tooth's root?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that cells near the root break it down, and that the adult tooth below sends signals. But exactly what starts it, and why each tooth goes at its own time, is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Could people one day grow a new adult tooth?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists in Japan are testing a medicine that may wake up the jaw's ability to grow a tooth. It has not yet been shown to work in people.

open_questions.q: Why do so many grown-ups have wisdom teeth that do not fit?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think it is because people now eat softer food, so jaws grow a little smaller. Others think genes matter more. They still argue about it.

open_questions.q: Which of the hundreds of kinds of mouth bacteria keep teeth healthy?
open_questions.why_open: Hundreds of kinds of bacteria live in a mouth. Only a few make lots of acid. Scientists are still finding out what the others do, and how they keep each other in balance.

Was that snack a helper or an acid time for your teeth?
Which teeth did you use to bite that? Which did you use to chew it?
Do you think a crocodile ever goes to a dentist? Why not?
If you could ask your adult teeth one question while they wait inside your jaw, what would you ask?
Why do you think a cold drink makes some people's teeth tingle?
What would you do with your next milk tooth when it falls out?
Why do you think the eggshell in vinegar went soft, but the one in water did not?

jokes.j: Why did the milk tooth leave the mouth?
jokes.a: It had to make room for a grown-up!

jokes.j: What does a dentist call her X-rays?
Why did the molar go to school?
jokes.a: To grind away at his lessons!

jokes.j: What did the tooth say to the dentist who was leaving?
jokes.a: Fill me in when you get back!

jokes.j: Why was the eggshell in vinegar so bubbly?
jokes.a: It was having a fizzy day!

jokes.j: What time do you go to the dentist?

maths.problem: A child has 20 milk teeth. A grown-up can have 32 adult teeth. How many more teeth can a grown-up have?
maths.explain: Count on from 20 to 32: 20 to 30 is 10, and 30 to 32 is 2 more. 10 and 2 make 12. So a grown-up can have 12 more teeth than a child.
maths.why_maths: Taking one number from the other shows exactly how many extra teeth come in as the jaw grows.

maths.problem: Your mouth has four quarters: top left, top right, bottom left and bottom right. Each quarter of a child's mouth has 5 milk teeth. How many milk teeth are there in all? A grown-up has 8 teeth in each quarter. How many is that?
maths.explain: 4 groups of 5 is 5, 10, 15, 20. 4 groups of 8 is 8, 16, 24, 32.
maths.why_maths: The mouth is made of four matching quarters, so counting one quarter and making four equal groups is quicker than counting every tooth.

maths.problem: Divya kept a sweet and sour tally for two days. On Monday she had 6 acid times. On Tuesday she ate her sweet with lunch and drank water after school, and had 3. How many fewer acid times did her teeth have on Tuesday? Which day was better for her teeth?
maths.explain: 6 take away 3 is 3. Tuesday had 3 fewer acid times, so acid had fewer chances to work on her teeth.
maths.context: This question is about the sweet and sour tally. You make a mark each time you eat or drink something sweet or sour in a day.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two tallies shows whether a change, like eating the sweet with lunch, really made a difference.

maths.problem: In the root test, the short-root pencil fell after 1, 2 and 1 taps. The long-root pencil fell after 9, 11 and 10 taps. Which pencil always needed more taps? Was any short-root try close to a long-root try?
maths.answer: The long-root pencil always needed more taps. No: the most taps for the short root was 2, and the fewest for the long root was 9.
maths.explain: Put the numbers in order: 1, 1, 2 for the short root and 9, 10, 11 for the long root. Even the biggest short-root number, 2, is much smaller than the smallest long-root number, 9. So the difference is not a fluke.
maths.context: This question is about the root test. You push two pencils into a block of atta dough, one deep and one shallow, and see which one falls over first.
maths.why_maths: Putting all the tries in order shows whether the two pencils really behave differently, or only by luck in one try.

maths.problem: Half of a child's 20 milk teeth are in the top jaw. How many are in the top jaw? How many are in the bottom jaw?
maths.answer: 10 in the top jaw and 10 in the bottom jaw.
maths.explain: Half of 20 is 10, because 10 and 10 make 20. The other half, 10, is in the bottom jaw.
maths.why_maths: Top and bottom teeth match each other, so splitting into halves helps you check a count in the mirror.

The eggshell test here compares five liquids and keeps a plain-water glass, so the child sees that acid, not sugar itself, softens the shell.

Ladder: sci.health.hygiene.L1 (the biscuit test, plaque bacteria and acid, the tooth worm story), sci.animals.animals-around-us.L1 (the chewing test) and sci.animals.animal-bodies.L2 (teeth map, cow's teeth). This unit does not repeat their experiments, stories or deep truths. It leads on from hygiene L1: there the child learned that bacteria make acid from leftovers; here the child tests what acid does to a hard material.
science: Primary dentition: 20 teeth (8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 molars), erupting from about 6 months to about 3 years. Permanent dentition: up to 32 (8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars, 12 molars). First permanent molars and incisors erupt at about 6 to 7. Any dental anatomy textbook.
Root resorption of primary teeth by odontoclasts as the successor tooth erupts.
Mamelons on newly erupted permanent incisors wear away with use.

Enamel is about 96% mineral (hydroxyapatite, a calcium phosphate) and is the hardest tissue in the body. Eggshell is mostly calcium carbonate, which gives off carbon dioxide in acid. Enamel dissolves in acid without fizzing.

Caries: acidogenic bacteria in plaque (for example Streptococcus mutans) ferment sugars to acids. Plaque pH falls after sugar and recovers over roughly 30 to 60 minutes (the Stephan curve). Frequency of sugar intake matters.

Fluoride history: F. S. McKay and G. V. Black on 'Colorado brown stain' (from 1901); M. C. Smith, E. M. Lantz and H. V. Smith, 'The cause of mottled enamel', Science 74 (1931); H. Trendley Dean's studies in the 1930s and 1940s.
Endemic dental fluorosis in India, including Nalgonda district (Telangana) and parts of Rajasthan.
A. Coppa and others, 'Early Neolithic tradition of dentistry', Nature 440 (2006): drilled molars from Mehrgarh, about 9,000 to 7,500 years old.
Elephants: six sets of molars in a lifetime. Sharks and crocodiles replace teeth many times.
Tooth regrowth: a clinical trial of an anti-USAG-1 antibody began in Japan in 2024. Results not yet known.
Shuo Yuan, chapter 'Jing Shen': Chang Cong and Laozi on the tongue and the teeth. Anguttara Nikaya 5.208 (Dantakattha Sutta).
sources.walkthrough: Every test was walked through for a city flat. A thumbnail-sized piece of eggshell in 3 tablespoons of white vinegar gives a steady stream of tiny bubbles within a minute, easy to see with a torch from the side. Lemon juice gives fewer, smaller bubbles. Water, milk and sugar water give none. After about 24 hours the vinegar piece is soft and bendy, often with only the thin inner skin left. Cowrie shells or seashells also fizz in vinegar, for families who do not use eggs. In the root test, a pencil pushed 1 cm into firm atta dough tips over with one or two light taps. One pushed 4 cm stands for many taps. The spine is the intro, the eggshell test and the torch tour (session 1, about 40 minutes, with the eggshell glasses left overnight), then the next-day eggshell check, the explanations, Roots and the quiz (session 2, about 35 minutes).

roots.context: We have learned about milk teeth and adult teeth, and tested what acid does to a hard eggshell. Now we ask what the eggshell test tells us about hardness, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In water, your eggshell stayed hard. In vinegar it fizzed, and by the next day it was soft and bendy. Tooth enamel is harder than eggshell, yet acid wears it away too. Hardness keeps a tooth from breaking when you bite, but it does not stop acid.
deep_truth.habit: We think the hardest thing is the safest thing. Hardness and standing up to acid are two different kinds of strength, and the test showed a hard shell giving way to a sour liquid.
deep_truth.evidence: In the eggshell test, the shell in water, milk and sugar water stayed hard. The shell in vinegar made bubbles at once and was soft by the next day. Enamel is harder than eggshell, but it is made with calcium too, and acid dissolves it slowly, though without bubbles.

three.who_am_i: Your adult teeth were already inside you when you were a baby. Part of the grown-up you will be is growing in you now.
three.what_is_life: Your body builds teeth, then takes away a milk tooth's root when it is time. Living things build, and take apart, to make room for what comes next.
three.what_is_this_world: Teeth, eggshells, seashells and limestone rock all hold calcium. The calcium in your smile came from food, and before that from soil and rock.

roots.thread: Calcium moves round the world. Rain wears calcium out of rock, and plants take calcium up from the soil. Animals eat the plants. A hen puts calcium into an eggshell, and a child's body puts calcium into enamel. Vinegar sets some of it free again, in bubbles of gas. Everything is conscious, the cells that build teeth too: they sense the signals around them and lay down each layer at the right time.

teachings.source: Shuo Yuan (Garden of Stories), compiled by Liu Xiang in China in the 1st century BCE: the story of Chang Cong and Laozi
teachings.teaching: An old teacher, Chang Cong, was dying. He opened his mouth and asked his student Laozi, 'Is my tongue still there?' 'Yes,' said Laozi. 'Are my teeth still there?' 'No.' 'Do you know why?' Laozi said, 'The tongue stays because it is soft. The teeth are gone because they are hard.'
teachings.link: The eggshell test showed the same surprise. The hardest thing does not always last longest. A hard shell gave way to a sour liquid that has no hardness at all.

teachings.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.208, the Dantakattha Sutta (the Buddha's teaching on tooth-sticks)
teachings.teaching: The Buddha named five good things that come from cleaning the teeth with a chewing stick, among them a mouth that does not smell bad and food that tastes good.
teachings.link: Long before anyone knew about bacteria or acid, people noticed that cleaning the teeth every day changes the mouth. Today we know one reason: cleaning takes away plaque, where the acid-making bacteria live.

science.text: Enamel is the hardest material in the human body. It is mostly a mineral with calcium in it, and acid can dissolve it.
Saliva and fluoride can put minerals back into the very first soft spot in enamel. A deep hole cannot be repaired this way.

other_view.view: They explain everything in the eggshell test with chemistry alone: acid reacts with calcium minerals and gives off a gas. They describe the cells that build teeth as following chemical signals, without any awareness.

practice.title: Feel the cold through the hard
practice.say: Take a small sip of cool water. Hold it in your mouth. Close your eyes. Can you feel the cold on your teeth? Enamel is hard, like stone. Yet you feel the cold through it. The feeling comes from the living pulp in the middle. Now swallow slowly. Run your tongue over your teeth, front to back. Each one is hard outside, and alive inside.

how_we_found_out.context: Why does most toothpaste have fluoride in it? This card tells the true story of how people found out.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1901, a young dentist called Frederick McKay began work in Colorado Springs, a town in the United States. He saw that many people there had brown spots on their teeth. Families worried that the spots meant weak, unhealthy teeth. But McKay noticed something odd. The spotted teeth had fewer holes than usual. For about 30 years, nobody could find the cause. In 1931, three scientists in Arizona found it. They were Margaret Cammack Smith, Edith Lantz and Howard Smith. They gave rats water from a town where children had spotted teeth, and the rats grew spotted teeth too. The cause was fluoride, a substance that was in the water. Later, a scientist called Trendley Dean showed that a small amount of fluoride in water means fewer cavities, while too much makes the spots. That is why most toothpaste has a little fluoride. In parts of India, such as Nalgonda in Telangana, the ground water has too much fluoride, and many people there have spotted teeth.
how_we_found_out.who: Frederick McKay, a dentist; Margaret Cammack Smith, Edith Lantz and Howard Smith, scientists in Arizona; and Trendley Dean
how_we_found_out.when: McKay began studying the spots in 1901. The Arizona scientists showed that fluoride caused them in 1931. Dean's studies of fluoride and cavities followed in the 1930s and 1940s.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That brown-spotted teeth must be weak teeth. The spotted teeth actually had fewer cavities. The spots came from a lot of fluoride, and a little fluoride turned out to protect teeth from acid.
